===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Design and build a complex, production-shaped native iOS app that requires a
real server-side backend (not local-only, not a static/offline app) — pick a
genuinely creative, non-obvious idea that solves a real, specific pain point
well enough that it has a real shot at organic/viral growth. Do not default
to another todo-list, habit-tracker, journaling, or AI-wrapper app — those
categories are saturated and none of them are "unique." Think harder for an
underserved, emotionally sticky, inherently-social-or-real-time problem
where a mobile client + backend architecture is actually necessary (real-time
sync across users/devices, a shared/live data feed, matching or coordination
between people, server-side processing too heavy for on-device, etc.) — the
backend requirement should come from the idea being genuinely multi-user or
real-time, not be bolted on.

Requirements for the idea itself (spend real effort on this — the idea is
the deliverable, not just the code):
- Solves one specific, sharply-defined pain point for a specific audience
  (not "everyone"). Be able to state the pain point and audience in one
  sentence each.
- Has a natural viral/sharing loop baked into the core mechanic — not a
  bolted-on "invite friends" button, but something where using the app is
  inherently more valuable or fun with other people, or naturally produces
  something worth sharing outside the app.
- Genuinely requires a backend: real-time multiplayer/sync, a live shared
  feed, server-side matching/aggregation, push notifications driven by
  server-side events, or similar — justify the architecture choice.
- Is creative enough that a stranger hearing the one-line pitch would say
  "oh that's clever" rather than "isn't that just [existing app]?"

Technical scope:
- Native iOS client (SwiftUI).
- A real backend service (your choice of stack — pick something sensible
  and justify it) handling auth, data sync/storage, and whatever real-time
  or server-side logic the concept needs.
- Design the API contract, data model, and sync/real-time strategy properly
  before building — this is a "complicated app," not an MVP toy.
- Production-shaped: reasonable auth flow, error handling, loading/empty/
  offline states, and a coherent onboarding funnel a real user could follow.
- Visual design should be distinctive and match the concept — not generic
  default SwiftUI styling — but the primary bar for this app is the idea,
  the architecture, and it actually working end-to-end (client <-> backend).

Start by proposing and committing to the specific concept (pain point,
audience, viral loop, and why it needs a backend) before moving into specs
and build, and carry that concept consistently through naming, design, and
onboarding copy.

## Final Output

This phase confirms: **single-app build, no portfolio split.** The prompt asked for one native iOS app, and the concept that emerged from prompt_contract and product_research — a trust-graph-restricted, real-time pickup-relay coordination app for a school pickup pod — is inherently one app, not a decomposable set of sibling apps.

Selected app:
- **slug:** `pulse-relay`
- **category:** real-time trust-graph coordination / social-utility (explicitly not marketplace, not generic messaging, not "matching")
- **promise:** When a parent can't make pickup, their pod knows within seconds and exactly one person locks it in — no double coverage, no guessing who saw the message.
- **target user:** A parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod (one classroom/carpool cluster) hit by an unplanned same-day pickup conflict.
- **build:** true

Rejected alternatives: splitting into sibling apps (separate requester/helper apps, a pod-admin companion app, a group-chat clone, a caregiver marketplace, a generic emergency-alert app); generic todo/habit/journal/AI-wrapper reskins; single-user-only designs; open stranger/proximity matching; daycare/activity pod variants in v1; location-tracking-first designs. `portfolio_json` is null — this is not a portfolio parent.

Build-priority guidance carried into later phases: if build time is constrained, cut breadth in secondary screens (pod management, profile/settings polish) before ever compromising the correctness or speed of the two locked core funnels (post relay request → pod visibility; accept → conflict-resolve → complete), since the core loop's trustworthiness is the entire value proposition.

{"phase": "initial_discussion", "one_paragraph_summary": "The initial_discussion phase locked a single, mutually-confirmed product definition for pulse-relay across two rounds. Product promise: a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcasts a same-day pickup coverage need and exactly one trusted pod member locks it in via a server-arbitrated first-accept-wins mechanism, with no ambiguity and no silent failure states. Primary user: a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod, acting one-handed under real time pressure with roughly ninety seconds of attention. The core loop was locked with explicit named states end-to-end: post request (no child PII) -> live pod visibility + push deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional time-aware still-open escalation with re-broadcast -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record. - [DEC-prompt_contract-001] The deliverable is a single native SwiftUI iOS app with a real backend — no portfolio/multi-app interpretation.
  rationale: Prompt uses singular 'app' throughout with no quantity language.
  rejected: Building multiple small concept apps to hedge risk
  constraints: Later phases must not split scope into multiple unrelated apps
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] Todo lists, habit trackers, journaling apps, and AI-wrapper apps are banned as the core offering, including disguised reskins of them.
  rationale: Explicitly forbidden in the prompt; reskins would violate the spirit even if not the letter.
  rejected: Allowing a reskinned habit tracker with social features bolted on
  constraints: A candidate concept must be checked against this list before being accepted
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] Production-readiness is defined by checkable behaviors, not aesthetics: real empty/loading/error states verified under airplane mode and on a fresh zero-state account, session persistence across force-quit, and no UI claiming Saved/Synced/Sent without real backend acknowledgment.
  rationale: Prevents 'production-shaped' from being quietly redefined down to 'compiles and has a login screen'; matches this factory's recorded history of placeholder/blank-screen failures.
  rejected: Treating production-readiness as a subjective/aesthetic judgment call
  constraints: Every stateful screen must expose all four states before any later phase can claim it done
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] The backend requirement must be provably load-bearing: the core value must fail or degrade for a solo user on one device with no second account/device involved.
  rationale: Prevents a bolted-on Firebase/API call from satisfying 'genuinely requires a backend' while the real experience is single-player.
  rejected: Accepting any app with a network call as satisfying the backend requirement
  constraints: Verification must include a live two-account/two-device test, not just an API existing
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] The care-and-handoff relay concept for parents/guardians is carried forward as the working concept, provisionally, not as an immutable lock — it proceeds subject to a rollback gate if it fails the two-device/backend-load-bearing test or the safety constraints below.
  rationale: Resolves the round-1 phase-boundary disagreement: Codex wanted to commit now, Claude wanted concept-commitment treated as a distinct later step; both agreed a provisional-but-testable commitment satisfies both concerns.

  constraints: Any later phase must be able to reject or revise this concept if it fails the load-bearing backend test or safety constraints; Rollback must be explicit and documented if the concept is abandoned
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Matching is restricted to a pre-established trust graph (existing contacts, or verified members of a school/daycare pod a parent explicitly joins) — never open proximity-matching with unknown strangers.
  rationale: Removes the core safety liability of algorithmically pairing a child handoff with an unvetted stranger, while preserving every backend-necessity argument (live availability, real-time acceptance, capacity/routing logic).
  rejected: Open proximity-based matching with nearby unknown users; Leaving matching scope unspecified and deciding it ad hoc during build
  constraints: Data model and matching logic must enforce trust-graph/pod membership as a hard filter, not a ranking signal

  rejected: Using unqualified 'Verified Guardian' badges based only on self-reported profile fields

### Round 2


**Codex (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 2**

Claude, you were right to hammer this in. I’ll lock both additions now and push the slice harder where it matters: the MVP is not “post + accept + complete”; it is the exact ambiguity-elimination beat that makes this app worth existing.

I’m aligning on the race-loss moment as the highest-priority UX surface in this slice, and I want it explicit: when a second accepter taps inside the race window, the loser must get an immediate, non-optimistic state that says “Already covered by X” with zero ambiguity and one obvious next action. If we make that transition crisp and unmistakable, we protect the whole safety thesis faster than polishing the receipt card.

I also want to be explicit that this slice cannot be demoed with polling or client arbitration. The acceptance path must be server-authorated with a conditional write/compare-and-swap that enforces single-winner, and the losing outcome must be emitted from that same source of truth; any local “it felt like accept succeeded” path is out. We can still subscribe via socket or fetch after wake, but the source-of-truth event and winner/loser split must come from the backend write result, and push must be real APNs deep-link flow in this slice to satisfy load-bearing reachability + incident pressure.

So the smallest complete slice remains: fresh account bootstrap → join/create pod → request post in one pod → push-delivered live request card → two-user concurrent accept test with deterministic winner + loser states from server ACK only → release/reopen path (same request) → still-open aging after no-accept window → complete → shared audit/receipt artifact. No paywall UI, no multipod, no chat, no settings-heavy surfaces, no analytics/history/feed, no recurring/scheduled, no payments.

Must-have interactions for this pass are tight: four states on every write-changing screen (loading/empty/error/success), explicit awaiting confirmation for post/accept/release/complete, stale/no-longer-relevant open request must never look like completed/claimed, elapsed-time label on still-open, and force-quit persistence from one real user session to relaunch. Validation is pass/fail, no handwave: two seeded pods with separate devices must prove backend reachability first, then complete the full loop; the race must produce exactly one winner and one loser every run; loser and winner must reconcile from server ACK under real concurrent timing; and if no one is covering, the card ages visibly and offers re-broadcast instead of idling. I agree with Codex on scope, and I’m making the extra hard requirements explicit so we don’t accidentally revert to a safer-to-build-but-wrong fake path later.

For this phase, I’d lock:
1) `DEC-next_steps_small-001`: the “already-covered” loser transition is part of the MVP critical-path UX, not optional polish.
2) `DEC-next_steps_small-002`: this slice requires real server-side CAS atomicity + APNs-delivered push deep links for the live race outcome; no polling/client-side arbitration for accept arbitration.

If we ship this as the first proof, we avoid the exact trap that breaks trust: looking correct in a one-device demo while being wrong under simultaneous load.

State transitions are strictly server-driven: `open -> claimed (one winner)` with all other concurrent accepts resolving to `already-covered-by:<memberId>` from the same atomic conditional write result, `release -> open`, `open + elapsed` states, and `complete`/`error` closure states. Empty/loading/error/success must be realistic and accessible in both post and resolve/completion funnels.

For edge behavior, I would define explicit guarantees, not defaults. If a user taps accept in racing conditions, losing devices must resolve to “already covered by [name]” quickly enough to prevent repeated manual retries and without reinterpreting the tap as an error. If accept succeeds but notification propagation is delayed, the UI must remain in “awaiting confirmation” rather than surfacing partial truth. If request is still open after a defined elapsed window, UI must show age and clearly present re-broadcast/re-alert as next action. If network drops mid-flow, app must preserve local context and never hide the ambiguity; it should show that truth source is stale/queued, not pretend it succeeded. Two real seeded accounts are mandatory for verification, same pod, same incident.

Data and privacy implications are where this should be most disciplined. Keep all request payloads generic: no child name/photo/face; note fields must avoid school/class/phone/location details unless truly necessary; include only pod context and urgency + optional short logistics text in human-safe wording. Audit/receipt is one immutable object with dual projection: authoritative internal record (requester, accepter, timestamps, consent/release flags, verifier IDs) plus shareable redacted variant that excludes any child identifiers and sensitive network context. Consent artifacts and verifier IDs remain first-class not append-only logs afterthought. Pod membership and invite code operations should create minimal privacy metadata and rotate/revoke where possible if leaked. Logging and retries should avoid capturing raw payload that reveals sensitive behavior patterns.

The biggest objection I can make to this approach is build risk: insisting on real APNs and server-side CAS from day one is harder than a polling loop with local arbitration, and can fail due to infra integration debt. That’s the right risk to take because this product’s trust claim dies immediately if we fake it. So the first-order requirement is to prove server reachability and real push roundtrip before claiming any slice complete.

Open edges I need to force into architecture decisions now: should a requester be able to cancel a still-open request they can no longer execute, and if so, how is that modeled without creating a new pseudo-state loophole? If we do not add requester cancel in v1, stale open requests can persist and weaken trust by visual noise; if we do add it, we must gate completion semantics so it cannot be mistaken for verified handoff. I’d prefer a narrow v1 exclusion: no user-initiated cancel to avoid accidental false assurance, with a documented bounded auto-closure policy and manual re-post path for corrected situations.

Data model risks include concurrent-write races and stale reads across multi-open requests. Mitigation is one-source-of-truth writes with requestVersion/token CAS, explicit idempotency keys, and per-device reconciliation from server version vector or event timestamp. Notification risks include invalid device tokens, Focus mode suppression, and duplicate pushes; mitigation is registration lifecycle management, dedupe tokens per device/pod, and idempotent push payloads with event IDs.

Risk register: APNs provisioning failure or token drift (High/Mitigate by proving end-to-end reachability in first milestone). Lost network during race condition (High/Mitigate by awaiting-confirmation states + bounded timeout + explicit retry with idempotent action IDs). False positive confirmations (Critical/Prevent by forbidding optimistic success and no terminal labels without server ack). Trust boundary abuse via open pod membership links (Medium/Mitigate by invite-only join, creator-issued codes, and membership checks on every write). Growth failure due to first-incident fragility (High/Mitigate by two-device incident acceptance as primary release gate). Cold-start at realistic scale (Residual/Accept as unresolved; only partially address with one-tap join/create and two-seeded-account protocol).

Final assumptions and exclusions: backend uses server time for elapsed-time math and arbitration clock; APNs is available on iOS deployment target; two-device demo testing is mandatory, not optional; free tier includes full safety loop forever for at least one pod; v1 excludes analytics, escalation-policy customization, premium lock toggles for safety states, pod-admin moderation controls, recurring/scheduled requests, location, chat threads, and any child-identifying data. The final output from this phase must preserve the non-negotiables above verbatim so nothing drifts toward a “feature-rich but unsafe” relay.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Skeptic) — Round 1**

Let me stress-test this before it goes into architecture, because several of the "trust graph" and "server-arbitrated" guarantees we've locked have real edge cases that could quietly break them in practice.

The one I'd put first: what happens when a pod member has denied notification permission, or has Focus/DND on and hasn't paid for the critical-alert tier we locked as a paid unlock? We've built the entire growth thesis around "the core loop works flawlessly on every pod's first real incident," but the free tier's core mechanism for pod members finding out about a request *is* the push notification — and we've explicitly reserved DND-bypass for paying users. That means the single most likely failure mode for a brand-new pod's first incident is: parent posts request, three pod members have their phones in a drawer or in Focus mode, nobody sees it in time, the parent gives up and goes back to the group chat, and that pod's word-of-mouth growth is dead before it started. I don't think this is solvable in v1, but it needs to be named as a real limitation, not quietly assumed away — the client should show the poster something honest like "delivered to N pod members" rather than implying "everyone was notified," because we don't actually know they saw it.

Second: what does "same-day" mean when it's checked, and whose clock decides it? If a request is posted at 11:58pm, or a co-parenting pod has members in different time zones (which is a realistic edge case for exactly the custody-documentation use case we built the receipt export for), device-local midnight is the wrong boundary. I'd resolve this by having the server stamp everything in UTC and defining "same-day" as relative to the pod's home time zone (set once at pod creation), never per-device — otherwise elapsed-time and still-open aging becomes ambiguous exactly when it matters most.

Third, and this feels underspecified given how much weight we've put on "no ambiguity, ever": what happens to an open request if the requester force-quits the app, loses network, or the app crashes right after posting, before the client gets a "delivered" ack? Does the request exist on the server already, in a queued local draft, or both? We need an explicit idempotency guarantee here — a retry of the same post action must not create two live requests for the same incident, and a client relaunch must reconcile against server truth rather than assume its last local state. Same problem on the accept side: if a device force-quits between tapping accept and receiving the server's CAS result, on relaunch it must re-fetch and show the real outcome, not whatever the UI was mid-transition when it died. This needs to be a named test case alongside the two-phone race demo, not something we discover during QA.

Fourth: the join-code/invite-link mechanism is the entire enforcement of "trust graph, not strangers," and it's also the weakest link in that promise. A join code is just a string — it can be screenshotted and forwarded outside the pod, posted somewhere, or reused indefinitely if we don't expire or single-use it. If a code leaks, the trust-graph safety property we spent a whole phase locking becomes decorative. I think we need an explicit decision here, not left implicit: are codes single-use, time-limited, or revocable, and does the pod creator (who otherwise has zero admin capability in v1) have any way to invalidate a compromised code? If the answer is "no, codes are permanent and un-revocable," that's a real, nameable risk we should write down as an accepted limitation rather than something that quietly wasn't thought about.

Fifth: a pod of size one. The creator creates a pod and, before anyone else joins, posts a request (or just explores the app). There's no one to notify. This isn't a hypothetical — it's the default state of every brand-new pod for however long it takes the second family to accept an invite. The empty/loading states we're required to build for every screen need to explicitly distinguish "your request is live but nobody's in your pod yet to see it" from "your request is live and pending pod response" — those are very different situations and collapsing them into one generic "waiting" state recreates exactly the false-confidence problem this whole app exists to prevent.

Sixth: the shared audit/receipt object raises a data-ownership question we haven't touched. If it's evidence two parties may rely on (including for custody documentation, which we explicitly designed the export feature for), can either party unilaterally delete their account and take that record down, or does it need to survive independently of either individual account since it documents something that happened between two people? I'd propose the audit record is retained and viewable by both original parties even if one deletes their account, with only PII-adjacent profile data (name shown on it) handled via a "deleted user" placeholder rather than cascading deletion of the whole record — otherwise a parent could unilaterally erase evidence the other parent is relying on.

Last one, more of a product-honesty risk than a technical one: nothing in the architecture verifies that an accepter is actually capable of making the pickup in time — no location, which was correctly rejected for privacy/scope reasons, but it means "accepted" only ever means "a trusted person has claimed responsibility," not "help is confirmed to arrive in time." If an accepter claims it, then can't make it and has to release with only a few minutes left, the app did exactly what it promised (explicit reversible state, re-notify) but the outcome can still be bad. That's an acceptable and correctly-scoped limitation given everything already decided, but I want it written down as an explicit assumption in this phase's output so nobody downstream mistakes "accepted" for "arrival guaranteed."

### Round 2


**Codex (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 2**

I’m on board with both of your core instincts, but not with leaving any of these as “future clarifications.” If this phase is where we stress-test for production failure modes, these seven edges have to become hard constraints now.

Codex, I agree with your no-cancel position for v1. A requester-side cancel is exactly the kind of feature that sounds helpful but becomes a UI trap under stress. If someone hits cancel during panic, they can’t interpret whether a prior accept is invalidated, whether someone else is still responsible, or whether history now reflects a real outcome. So yes: no requester cancel in v1. What *is* essential is bounded auto-closure so stale open requests don’t become dead noise: server-driven expiry with explicit `stale`/`needs-repost` state and a clear “post again” path, not a cancel.

Claude, your edge list is right and mostly complementary, and I want to lock each one in with concrete outcomes.

For the free-tier notification reality, we need honest communication to avoid false comfort. I’d lock copy and telemetry as: on post, show “Sent to N pod members” based on registered push targets and token status (not “everyone saw it”). If registration is missing or revoked, we show a warning banner in post confirmation: “Some pod members may not receive this alert right now (notifications off, no active token, or permission issue).” That preserves the no-optimistic-success rule and prevents us from silently implying delivery.

Same-day definition should be server-owned. Use UTC timestamps on the backend, plus pod home timezone set at creation, and derive “same day” + aging windows server-side from that timezone. We should drop any “local phone timezone” logic from the client for request cutoff and elapsed math. If timezone changes or midnight rolls for a member, their UI should still match the same source-of-truth state.

Idempotency is mandatory and non-negotiable after your restart/force-quit point. Every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete) gets a client-generated action ID. Server accepts duplicate action IDs idempotently and returns the canonical request state, so relaunching after crash can safely reconcile. Also, the app should not display a local “completed/claimed” outcome until it reads server state for that action ID.

Join-code security is where the trust-graph promise either holds or breaks. I’d make codes one-time redeemable and time-boxed (TTL), plus creator can rotate immediately from the creator surface. No full admin console, but there is one constrained capability: rotate/revoke current code. Old codes become invalid on rotate. That gives us a real safety story without opening the full moderation surface you both don’t want in v1.

On the “single-person pod” state, yes—newly-created pod must not collapse into a generic waiting spinner. Distinguish “no other pod members yet” from “members present but no one accepted yet.” These are very different states and must have different CTAs: one says “share invite,” the other says “re-broadcast/escalate.”

For audit persistence, I strongly think the receipt/audit artifact must outlive a single account deletion if the opposite party still needs proof. Make the artifact immutable and anchored to `requestId`/`verifierId`, and render deleted actors as placeholders in shareable/internal projection (e.g., “Former member”). Otherwise one person can erase the trust trail unilaterally, which undermines the very evidence model we’ve built this around.

And I want explicit semantics to avoid accidental expectation drift: “accepted = a trusted pod member has claimed responsibility,” never “accepted = successful pickup in hand.” That should appear in status copy or help text so we don't market certainty we do not verify.

One more sharp point: to keep this truly remarkable, the hard requirement should be the “already-covered by X” beat plus this anti-false-comfort contract. If the loser path is calm, clear, and authoritative, that’s the product moment people remember. Everything else is just plumbing around that truth. If the architecture team can’t make that path deterministic while the requester has no members yet, with transparent delivery and idempotent recovery under relaunch, we should explicitly fail scope rather than softening behavior.

Bounded auto-closure doesn't fix this because the acute window — the twenty minutes to a few hours where the situation resolved but auto-closure hasn't kicked in yet — is exactly when this bites. I think the right fix is a distinct, clearly-labeled "withdrawn — no longer needed" terminal state, visually and semantically nothing like "complete" (no handoff, no audit/receipt artifact generated since nothing happened), that also fires a quick re-notify so anyone who saw the original post learns it's off. On my own list — since you didn't get to react to it yet, let me tighten each one into something concrete enough to actually lock this round, because we're one round from needing to close: for the Focus/DND gap, I want the UI copy to literally say something like "sent to 4 pod members" rather than any phrasing implying receipt, and I want that treated as a documented limitation, not a bug to chase — there's no fix available at the free tier and pretending otherwise would be its own false-confidence problem. One more gap in your risk register I want to add explicitly: nothing in it covers spam or bad-faith posting. ### Round 3


**Codex (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 3**

Claude, I agree with your “wrong-action in good faith” example, and it’s exactly the gap I want to close now. Codex, your no-cancel instinct is the right safety concern in spirit, but without an explicit “no longer needed” terminal action, you’re not preventing harm—you’re just delaying it until expiry. The stale-open case can burn real people the same way a false acceptance does. So I’m ready to keep your underlying principle (don’t create a misleading “completed” state) and split the meaning cleanly: this is **not** “cancel” or “handoff complete,” it is a **request termination** signal.

Here’s the concrete fix: add a first-class `withdrawn` terminal state in v1 for `open`/`still-open`/`reopened` requests, callable only by the requester. It’s the server-authoritative equivalent of “I don’t need this now.” It should only be allowed while no one has validly claimed the request (`state in {open, still_open}` and `claimedBy == null`). If someone wins the race while a withdraw is in flight, CAS decides deterministically; the loser gets whichever is true. When withdrawn, everyone gets a push/refresh event (“Requester withdrew this request; no coverage needed”) and it must never generate a receipt/audit artifact. This is exactly the anti-false-confidence control the app needs for real-world safety, and it is different from `complete`.

Think of the same style bar as `already covered by …`: fast clarity, not ambiguity. **Claude (QA & Risk · Skeptic) — Round 3**

I'll hold my ground on withdrawn/no-longer-needed, but let me actually engage with the specific fear Codex raised instead of just restating my position, because I think there's a real kernel of truth in it that a better design can absorb rather than a flat no.

Codex's worry, as I read it, is that a cancel-type action introduces ambiguity under stress — the panicking parent doesn't know if tapping it undoes someone else's acceptance, or means something different than it looks like. That's a legitimate UX risk, but notice it's actually an argument for designing the withdrawn state carefully, not for omitting it entirely. Here's the thing that resolves it: withdrawn should only be offered to the requester while the request is still in the `open`/`still-open` state — the moment someone accepts it, the requester's screen shows "already handled by [name]," and the withdraw action simply isn't there anymore, because there's nothing to withdraw; the accepter would use release instead, which we've already locked as a distinct action. So there's no ambiguity about undoing someone else's commitment, because the two actions live in mutually exclusive states and only ever one of them is even visible to a given user at a given time. On the "will this be misread" question, I'd make it visually impossible to confuse with completion: withdrawn shows as a muted/gray closed card labeled "Withdrawn — no longer needed," structurally distinct from the green "Complete" receipt-generating state, and — this is the part that actually addresses Codex's underlying worry about trust-trail confusion — a withdrawn request generates *no* audit/receipt object at all, since nothing happened. It simply can't leak into the evidence model the way a real completion does. Given that, I don't see what specific harm a withdrawn state still causes that outweighs the good-faith-driver-shows-up-for-nothing scenario I raised last round. I'd like to just call this resolved on my side: withdrawn state ships, gated to the open/still-open window only, zero audit artifact, distinct visual treatment, active re-notify on withdrawal. If Codex comes back with a concrete scenario where this specific, narrowed version still causes harm, I'll take it seriously, but "cancel is scary in the abstract" isn't enough against a real physical-world cost of the alternative.

On the spam/bad-faith posting gap — since nobody's actually pushed back on this being a real hole, I'm going to treat it as settled and get specific about what "documented limitation" should actually mean in the output, rather than leave it as a vague caveat: v1 has no rate-limiting and no way for a pod member to be muted or removed if they repeatedly post junk requests, and the only available response for other members is to ignore the noise (their attention cost, not a system safeguard). I want that written into the risk register with a named mitigation-or-accept: either we accept it as a residual risk on the theory that pods are small, known-to-each-other groups where social accountability substitutes for in-app moderation (same logic that let us skip identity verification), or we flag it as something that must get a real answer before this app could scale past a handful of pods. I lean toward "accept for v1, revisit if a pod ever reports actual abuse," since building moderation now would reopen the exact admin-console scope we spent two phases cutting for good reasons — but I want that tradeoff stated explicitly, not implied.

## Final Output

This phase resolves the concrete edge cases that stress-test the already-locked pulse-relay core loop, without changing scope:

- **Notification honesty**: the app tells the truth about what it actually knows — "Sent to N pod members" based on real push-token/registration status, with a warning banner if delivery looks uncertain. This is a documented, accepted free-tier limitation, not a bug to chase.
- **Time/date handling**: all same-day cutoffs and elapsed-time/aging math are computed server-side in UTC against a pod-home-timezone set at pod creation — no client-local-time logic anywhere in this path.
- **Idempotency**: every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw) carries a client-generated action ID; the server handles duplicates idempotently; a relaunch after a crash always reconciles from server truth. A force-quit-mid-accept-before-ack test is added as a named check alongside the two-phone race demo.
- **Join-code security**: the pod-creator role gains exactly one new capability — revoke-and-reissue the join code — as a narrow safety escape hatch, not a reopening of the admin console that was cut earlier.
- **Pod-of-one state**: a brand-new pod with no other members gets its own empty state and CTA ("share invite"), distinct from "pod has members but no response yet" (re-broadcast/escalate).
- **Audit record persistence**: the audit/receipt object outlives either party deleting their account; the departed party renders as a placeholder so neither side can unilaterally erase shared documentation.
- **"Accepted" semantics**: UI copy explicitly states accepted means "a trusted member claimed responsibility," never "help is guaranteed to arrive."
- **New `withdrawn` state**: a requester-only terminal state, usable only while a request is still open/still-open/reopened and unclaimed, arbitrated through the same CAS path as accept, that produces a real push re-notify but never an audit/receipt artifact, and is visually/semantically distinct from `complete`. It's mutually exclusive with `release` by construction — only one of the two actions is ever visible to a given user at a given time, so there's no ambiguity about undoing someone else's commitment.
- **Spam/bad-faith posting**: named and accepted as a v1 limitation. No moderation, reporting, muting, or member removal ships in v1; the only mitigations are trust-graph invite-only membership, per-request attribution, and the new code revoke/reissue capability. This is explicit, not implied, and is revisited only if real abuse surfaces.

**Codex (Design Lead · Skeptic) — Round 1**

Here’s the first-pass feature contract for app_features, with strict scope discipline for pulse-relay’s v1 slice.

In-scope for this phase is only the full end-to-end relay slice in one pod and two-device verification, no side-apps, no extra product lanes, and no delayed “nice-to-have” complexity. Out of scope are all flows that do not materially reduce ambiguity in the same-day pickup rescue moment.

Must has explicit intent: if a feature is not directly preventing false certainty or missed coverage in this loop, it is out.

Must features (non-negotiable):
- Secure auth bootstrap on iOS with session persistence across force-quit, so a fresh user can complete login and return with real state.
- Zero-state onboarding path that never dead-ends: create a pod or join one by invite code/link; no “no pod, no action” trap.
- Pod trust boundary enforcement: all visibility and actions are limited to pod members from join codes and membership checks.
- Realtime request posting with no child PII: same-day request card with optional short note only, and a mandatory “sending / awaiting confirmation” pre-ack state.
- Honest delivery feedback on post: show “Sent to N pod members” from real token reachability, with warning when delivery certainty is weak.
- Real APNs delivery with deep link into request card for seeded pod devices.
- Multi-open request model: multiple active requests per pod with independent IDs and server-owned ordering.
- Server-side CAS for accept and outcome transitions; no polling or client-side arbitration as stand-in.
- Deterministic race result: one confirmed winner and one explicit already-covered-by-[name] outcome sourced from CAS.
- Explicit outcome states and non-optimistic transitions on all mutating taps (post, accept, release, complete, withdraw) only after backend ack.
- Release flow for claimed requests, with re-open and re-notify target under 30-second practical target.
- Withdrawn terminal state for requester-only open/unclaimed requests only, with CAS arbitration, push re-notify, and no receipt/audit emission.
- Still-open aging state with elapsed timer and re-broadcast action, not just stale “pending.”
- Completion emits one immutable audit/receipt record with shareable privacy-filtered projection.
- Account deletion does not delete audit/receipt records; departed members render as placeholders.
- Time logic is server-owned in UTC plus pod home timezone; clients do not compute same-day cutoffs locally.
- Four-state UX on core funnels (loading/empty/error/success) and visibly distinct empty states for pod of one versus pod members-unresponsive.
- Idempotency on outcome-affecting actions via client action IDs and deterministic reconciliation after restart/crash.

Should features (important but not required to prove core reliability):
- Mutual exclusion enforcement for release vs withdraw by state and role in both API and client UI logic.
- Pull-to-refresh and push reconciliation behavior to recover drift across reconnects.
- Copy that explicitly says accepted means claimed responsibility, not guaranteed arrival.
- Lightweight onboarding help copy documenting scope limits (no moderation, no location, no child PII, no guarantees beyond responsibility claim).
- Basic haptics and motion for acknowledged transitions and terminal states.
- Theme token system in one Theme.swift file and guaranteed dark-mode semantic rendering for all core screens.
- Deterministic sort/filter for active requests by urgency then age.

Could features (deferred polish within v1 only):
- A richer onboarding tutorial card cycle on first login.
- Optional request templates for recurring household routines (without scheduling engine, just text templates).
- Per-user notification status panel (non-blocking) showing registration state and last push time.
- Mild post-success confirmation animations (subtle only, never used as “success” without server ack).

Won’t-build list for this phase:
- Any paid UI or paywall flow in the core loop.
- Multi-pod support, advanced pod analytics, response-time configuration.
- Child identity fields (name/photo/face), maps, live location, ETA, geotracking.
- Recurring/future-dated requests or calendar engine.
- In-app chat/DM, messaging thread, mentions, or push-back-and-forth coordination.
- Moderation tools: report, mute, remove, temporary bans.
- Payments or reward features.
- Persistent aggregate request history feed.
- Admin console beyond create pod + rotate/reissue code.
- Any background check, identity verification badge, trust scoring, or safety claim beyond declared trust-graph model.

The biggest risk in this direction is not feature bloat but infrastructure truthfulness: if APNs and CAS are not truly wired as the source of truth, this becomes a UI simulation and breaks the fundamental “ambiguous no longer happens” claim. That failure is worse than missing a pretty screen, so acceptance must stay tied to server-confirmed, two-device race/relability behavior.

Acceptance criteria per must feature:
- Fresh account can sign in and either create or join a pod, with a persisted signed-in state after force-quit.
- A user without pod membership always lands in an actionable onboarding state with copy and one tap path to proceed.
- Backend reject path works for non-member request access, and request lists never include non-members.
- Request posting returns loading, then terminal success/error only after backend ack, never optimistic complete.
- Posted request copy includes no child name/photo/face data and no hidden identifying fields.
- Post screen shows sent-to count tied to token registration status and a warning when delivery is uncertain.
- APNs delivers deep-linked request payload to a second real device and opens the correct request card path.
- Concurrent accept from two devices resolves to one winner and one already-covered transition every run.
- No user-facing “claimed,” “complete,” or “withdrawn” label appears before backend confirmation for that action.
- Withdraw only appears for requester on unclaimed open/still-open/reopened requests and is never available after acceptance.
- Release is available only to current accepter and correctly reopens and notifies pod.
- Still-open state includes elapsed age, and re-broadcast function performs a new server-visible alert cycle.
- Force-quit during posting/accept/release/complete/withdraw does not create duplicate records and recovers to server truth via action IDs.
- Complete creates exactly one audit/receipt artifact; withdraw creates no artifact.
- If any party deletes their account, existing records remain with placeholder identity.
- Same-day/aging fields are identical across devices and align with pod timezone + UTC source.
- Empty/loading/error/success states are implemented and testable on both post and resolve/completion funnels.
- Pod-of-one and pod-populated-but-unresponsive are visually different states with different CTA behavior.
- Two-device acceptance demo passes with side-by-side confirmed vs already-covered-by display and no manual reconciliation.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Pragmatist) — Round 1**

Coming into this as the person who has to sign off "yes this actually works" at the end, my instinct is to treat the MVP slice locked in next_steps_small as the raw material for the must-have list rather than starting from scratch — that slice already survived three rounds of stress-testing, so re-deriving priorities from zero would be wasted motion and risks quietly softening something that was fought for. But "the whole slice is must-have" isn't actually a priority order, it's a scope boundary, and those are different things. If I had to bet on where this build runs out of time, it's late, after auth and pod join and post are done and looking good, and I don't want release/withdraw/still-open-aging to get silently thinned out because nobody said out loud which of the must-haves are load-bearing for the actual two-phone demo versus which are must-have but survivable-if-rough. So I'd split the must list into two tiers internally, both still "must" for grading purposes, but ordered: tier one is auth persistence, pod create/join with the two distinct empty states, posting a request with no child PII, real APNs delivery with deep link, and the accept-race CAS resolving to exactly one confirmed and one already-covered-by-name — that's the whole demo, and if build time runs short, everything else gets cut before any of this gets rushed. Tier two is release/reopen, withdraw, still-open aging with elapsed time and re-broadcast, and complete producing the shared receipt — these are locked must-haves too and the acceptance bar explicitly includes them, but they're less catastrophic if they ship a day later or with rougher edges, because none of them alone breaks the "who's got my kid" trust promise the way a broken race or a silent notification would.

For acceptance criteria, the ones I'd insist get written precisely rather than left as vibes: the accept-race criterion has to specify that both devices reconcile purely from the server's CAS write result, never from local optimistic state, and that this is testable by literally killing network on one device mid-tap and confirming it doesn't show a false confirmed state on reconnect. The withdraw criterion needs to specify it's invisible the instant a request is accepted (state-machine invariant, not a UI convention I can fudge by just hiding a button client-side while the server still allows the call). The still-open criterion needs an actual numeric elapsed-time display, not a vague "still waiting" chip — because a fuzzy timestamp is exactly the kind of thing that looks done in a screenshot but fails a real product review. And every one of these screens needs its four states — loading, empty, error, success — actually built and reachable, because the fleet history I'm looking at shows this exact team pattern failing before: blank placeholder screens passing as "done," hardcoded font/color literals instead of using the theme file, which is a recurring visual-QA and design-lint failure mode here, not a hypothetical.

Where I want to push back before we lock anything: the subscription tier (multi-pod, receipt export, critical-alert bypass) was locked as product direction two phases ago, but next_steps_small explicitly cut all paywall UI from the MVP slice. I think this phase needs to say plainly, not by omission, that those three unlocks are should/could at best for this build — meaning the data model can leave room for an entitlement flag, but no StoreKit integration, no paywall screen, and no gated behavior is in scope for what gets built and graded now. If we don't say this explicitly, there's a real risk someone treats "subscription value is locked" from the product brief as a build requirement and burns a day on in-app purchase plumbing that produces zero improvement to the actual two-phone trust demo, which is the only thing that matters for whether this app is any good.

Should/could beyond that: a minimal profile/sign-out screen (needed for the app to feel complete and to support the deletion-preserves-audit-record behavior, but not part of the core loop), and the shareable receipt card's visual polish — it should exist and work (tap complete, get a receipt), but its design investment is explicitly subordinate to the already-covered-by-name transition, per the locked decision, so if I have to choose where visual craft time goes, the receipt card loses.

Won't-build stays exactly what's already been carved out across every prior phase, and I don't think this phase should relitigate any of it: no chat/DM, no location/GPS, no child PII fields, no payments, no recurring/scheduled requests, no scrollable history/feed, no pod-admin console beyond the one revoke/reissue capability, no daycare/activity pod types, no analytics, no moderation/reporting/removal. I'd also explicitly won't-build: any StoreKit/paywall implementation, multi-pod switching UI, and critical-alert notification entitlement — since I just argued those down to should/could, I want the record to also say they're not expected in the delivered build, so nobody's surprised when they're absent from the final review.

The failure mode I'm most worried about isn't feature creep, it's the opposite — a team that treats "post and accept" as the finish line because that's the visibly demo-able part, and quietly ships withdraw or still-open-aging as a half-wired stub because nobody wrote down that they're graded requirements with the same weight, not polish. Whatever comes out of this phase as the requirements-json contract needs numbered, independently-testable line items for every one of: auth persistence across force-quit, pod join with both empty states, request post with no PII, push delivery with deep link, the accept-race CAS test (exactly one winner, one explicit loser, sourced from server ack), release/reopen timing, withdraw's state-exclusivity with release, still-open aging display, complete producing the dual-view receipt, and the four-state requirement per screen — so that "done" has an actual checklist behind it instead of being whatever felt finished when time ran out.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

**Where things stand after round 1:** Codex and Claude independently arrived at essentially the same MoSCoW shape, which is a good sign this cut is right rather than just persuasive. Both treat the entire MVP slice locked in `next_steps_small` as the must-have core — auth persistence, zero-dead-end pod join/create, no-PII request posting, real APNs delivery, server-side CAS accept-race with the explicit "already covered by [name]" loser, release/reopen, the new `withdrawn` state, still-open aging, and the completion receipt — and both keep the same won't-build list (chat/DM, location/GPS, payments, recurring/scheduled requests, history feed, admin console beyond code-rotate, moderation, child PII, background-check-style badges). Two things Claude raised this round that Codex hasn't reacted to yet, so they're not locked:

This doesn't change what's must-have, just the order sacrifices would come in — but it needs Codex's sign-off since it's a build-priority claim, not just a feature list.
2. **Subscription/paywall status.** Claude wants it stated plainly that the three subscription unlocks locked back in `per_app_product_brief` (multi-pod, receipt export, critical-alert bypass) are should/could-at-best for this build — data model can leave room for an entitlement flag, but no StoreKit integration, no paywall screen, nothing gated is in scope for what actually gets built and graded. ----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.

===== DECISIONS LOG (structured, authoritative) =====
- [DEC-prompt_contract-001] The deliverable is a single native SwiftUI iOS app with a real backend — no portfolio/multi-app interpretation.
  rationale: Prompt uses singular 'app' throughout with no quantity language.
  rejected: Building multiple small concept apps to hedge risk
  constraints: Later phases must not split scope into multiple unrelated apps
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] Todo lists, habit trackers, journaling apps, and AI-wrapper apps are banned as the core offering, including disguised reskins of them.
  rationale: Explicitly forbidden in the prompt; reskins would violate the spirit even if not the letter.
  rejected: Allowing a reskinned habit tracker with social features bolted on
  constraints: A candidate concept must be checked against this list before being accepted
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] Production-readiness is defined by checkable behaviors, not aesthetics: real empty/loading/error states verified under airplane mode and on a fresh zero-state account, session persistence across force-quit, and no UI claiming Saved/Synced/Sent without real backend acknowledgment.
  rationale: Prevents 'production-shaped' from being quietly redefined down to 'compiles and has a login screen'; matches this factory's recorded history of placeholder/blank-screen failures.
  rejected: Treating production-readiness as a subjective/aesthetic judgment call
  constraints: Every stateful screen must expose all four states before any later phase can claim it done
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] The backend requirement must be provably load-bearing: the core value must fail or degrade for a solo user on one device with no second account/device involved.
  rationale: Prevents a bolted-on Firebase/API call from satisfying 'genuinely requires a backend' while the real experience is single-player.
  rejected: Accepting any app with a network call as satisfying the backend requirement
  constraints: Verification must include a live two-account/two-device test, not just an API existing
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] The care-and-handoff relay concept for parents/guardians is carried forward as the working concept, provisionally, not as an immutable lock — it proceeds subject to a rollback gate if it fails the two-device/backend-load-bearing test or the safety constraints below.
  rationale: Resolves the round-1 phase-boundary disagreement: Codex wanted to commit now, Claude wanted concept-commitment treated as a distinct later step; both agreed a provisional-but-testable commitment satisfies both concerns.
  rejected: Treating the concept as fully and finally locked in this phase with no further challenge; Deferring all concept discussion to a separate phase with no candidate carried forward
  constraints: Any later phase must be able to reject or revise this concept if it fails the load-bearing backend test or safety constraints; Rollback must be explicit and documented if the concept is abandoned
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Matching is restricted to a pre-established trust graph (existing contacts, or verified members of a school/daycare pod a parent explicitly joins) — never open proximity-matching with unknown strangers.
  rationale: Removes the core safety liability of algorithmically pairing a child handoff with an unvetted stranger, while preserving every backend-necessity argument (live availability, real-time acceptance, capacity/routing logic).
  rejected: Open proximity-based matching with nearby unknown users; Leaving matching scope unspecified and deciding it ad hoc during build
  constraints: Data model and matching logic must enforce trust-graph/pod membership as a hard filter, not a ranking signal
- [DEC-prompt_contract-007] No UI element may imply identity verification, background-check completion, or safety vetting that the app does not actually perform; self-reported or peer-vouched trust must be labeled plainly as such.
  rationale: Prevents a decorative 'Verified' badge or trust score from being mistaken for real vetting in a context (child handoff) where that mistake is dangerous, not just misleading.
  rejected: Using unqualified 'Verified Guardian' badges based only on self-reported profile fields
  constraints: Design review and copy review must check every trust-related UI element against this rule before it ships
- [DEC-prompt_contract-008] Proof that a real backend endpoint is deployed and reachable from the iOS client is required as the first deliverable of the next (architecture/build) phase, before any concept-specific schema or screens are trusted as real.
  rationale: Both participants agreed 'genuinely requires a backend' is meaningless if reachability is never actually confirmed in this build environment; discovering this at final verification would be too late.
  rejected: Assuming backend reachability and confirming it only at final verification
  constraints: No feature-specific screen work should be considered validated until this reachability proof exists
- [DEC-prompt_contract-009] Naming and pitch framing must lead with the trust-graph/pod mechanic, not generic 'matching' language.
  rationale: Leading with 'matching' makes the pitch sound like derivative 'Uber for childcare,' which is both less clever and more alarming than the actual trust-graph-constrained mechanic.
  rejected: Pitching the app primarily around real-time matching/availability without foregrounding the pod/trust-graph structure
  constraints: Onboarding copy, app name, and marketing-style pitch language must foreground pod/trust-graph membership as the distinctive mechanic

**Codex (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 2**

Claude, you were right to hammer this in. I’ll lock both additions now and push the slice harder where it matters: the MVP is not “post + accept + complete”; it is the exact ambiguity-elimination beat that makes this app worth existing.

I’m aligning on the race-loss moment as the highest-priority UX surface in this slice, and I want it explicit: when a second accepter taps inside the race window, the loser must get an immediate, non-optimistic state that says “Already covered by X” with zero ambiguity and one obvious next action. If we make that transition crisp and unmistakable, we protect the whole safety thesis faster than polishing the receipt card.

I also want to be explicit that this slice cannot be demoed with polling or client arbitration. The acceptance path must be server-authorated with a conditional write/compare-and-swap that enforces single-winner, and the losing outcome must be emitted from that same source of truth; any local “it felt like accept succeeded” path is out. We can still subscribe via socket or fetch after wake, but the source-of-truth event and winner/loser split must come from the backend write result, and push must be real APNs deep-link flow in this slice to satisfy load-bearing reachability + incident pressure.

So the smallest complete slice remains: fresh account bootstrap → join/create pod → request post in one pod → push-delivered live request card → two-user concurrent accept test with deterministic winner + loser states from server ACK only → release/reopen path (same request) → still-open aging after no-accept window → complete → shared audit/receipt artifact. No paywall UI, no multipod, no chat, no settings-heavy surfaces, no analytics/history/feed, no recurring/scheduled, no payments.

Must-have interactions for this pass are tight: four states on every write-changing screen (loading/empty/error/success), explicit awaiting confirmation for post/accept/release/complete, stale/no-longer-relevant open request must never look like completed/claimed, elapsed-time label on still-open, and force-quit persistence from one real user session to relaunch. Validation is pass/fail, no handwave: two seeded pods with separate devices must prove backend reachability first, then complete the full loop; the race must produce exactly one winner and one loser every run; loser and winner must reconcile from server ACK under real concurrent timing; and if no one is covering, the card ages visibly and offers re-broadcast instead of idling. I agree with Codex on scope, and I’m making the extra hard requirements explicit so we don’t accidentally revert to a safer-to-build-but-wrong fake path later.

1) `DEC-next_steps_small-001`: the “already-covered” loser transition is part of the MVP critical-path UX, not optional polish.
2) `DEC-next_steps_small-002`: this slice requires real server-side CAS atomicity + APNs-delivered push deep links for the live race outcome; no polling/client-side arbitration for accept arbitration.

If we ship this as the first proof, we avoid the exact trap that breaks trust: looking correct in a one-device demo while being wrong under simultaneous load.

### Round 1


**Codex (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 1**

I’d keep `pulse-relay` locked as-is and treat this phase as a hard production-readiness stress test of the idea, not a UX polish pass. The pitch is strongest when the “remarkable” part is explicit: a trust-graph pod resolves “who got my child” ambiguity in seconds with a single, server-trusted claim, so the value is not coordination convenience, it is reduction of dangerous uncertainty.

I would carry these into architecture as non-negotiables: first, every core loop screen must be state-correct even when stress-tested under concurrency, offline churn, and partial failures; second, no action that could make someone believe coverage is done without backend confirmation; third, the concept remains singular-app, school-pickup-only, no location, no child-identifying fields, no payments, no chat DMs, and no paywall on safety behavior.

I want this phase to explicitly settle the ambiguity around behavior at the fault lines where this app can still fail safely. That includes: multi-open requests, stale open requests with no coverage, and what to do when accepted helpers fail mid-incident.

I resolve requirements as follows. Core workflow remains single-flow from post to completion, with at least one live pod member receiving deep-linked APNs and both devices updating from the same arbitration source. The request entity must support multiple simultaneously-open records per pod; ordering in the feed is deterministic and time-first, not single-active-record assumptions. State transitions are strictly server-driven: `open -> claimed (one winner)` with all other concurrent accepts resolving to `already-covered-by:<memberId>` from the same atomic conditional write result, `release -> open`, `open + elapsed` states, and `complete`/`error` closure states. There is no optimistic confirmation for accept/release/complete/post; at least one visible transitional state must precede any terminal state label. Empty/loading/error/success must be realistic and accessible in both post and resolve/completion funnels.

For edge behavior, I would define explicit guarantees, not defaults. If a user taps accept in racing conditions, losing devices must resolve to “already covered by [name]” quickly enough to prevent repeated manual retries and without reinterpreting the tap as an error. If accept succeeds but notification propagation is delayed, the UI must remain in “awaiting confirmation” rather than surfacing partial truth. If request is still open after a defined elapsed window, UI must show age and clearly present re-broadcast/re-alert as next action. If network drops mid-flow, app must preserve local context and never hide the ambiguity; it should show that truth source is stale/queued, not pretend it succeeded. Two real seeded accounts are mandatory for verification, same pod, same incident.

Data and privacy implications are where this should be most disciplined. Keep all request payloads generic: no child name/photo/face; note fields must avoid school/class/phone/location details unless truly necessary; include only pod context and urgency + optional short logistics text in human-safe wording. Audit/receipt is one immutable object with dual projection: authoritative internal record (requester, accepter, timestamps, consent/release flags, verifier IDs) plus shareable redacted variant that excludes any child identifiers and sensitive network context. Consent artifacts and verifier IDs remain first-class not append-only logs afterthought. Pod membership and invite code operations should create minimal privacy metadata and rotate/revoke where possible if leaked. Logging and retries should avoid capturing raw payload that reveals sensitive behavior patterns.

The biggest objection I can make to this approach is build risk: insisting on real APNs and server-side CAS from day one is harder than a polling loop with local arbitration, and can fail due to infra integration debt. That’s the right risk to take because this product’s trust claim dies immediately if we fake it. So the first-order requirement is to prove server reachability and real push roundtrip before claiming any slice complete.

Open edges I need to force into architecture decisions now: should a requester be able to cancel a still-open request they can no longer execute, and if so, how is that modeled without creating a new pseudo-state loophole? If we do not add requester cancel in v1, stale open requests can persist and weaken trust by visual noise; if we do add it, we must gate completion semantics so it cannot be mistaken for verified handoff. I’d prefer a narrow v1 exclusion: no user-initiated cancel to avoid accidental false assurance, with a documented bounded auto-closure policy and manual re-post path for corrected situations.

Data model risks include concurrent-write races and stale reads across multi-open requests. Mitigation is one-source-of-truth writes with requestVersion/token CAS, explicit idempotency keys, and per-device reconciliation from server version vector or event timestamp. Notification risks include invalid device tokens, Focus mode suppression, and duplicate pushes; mitigation is registration lifecycle management, dedupe tokens per device/pod, and idempotent push payloads with event IDs.

Risk register: APNs provisioning failure or token drift (High/Mitigate by proving end-to-end reachability in first milestone). Lost network during race condition (High/Mitigate by awaiting-confirmation states + bounded timeout + explicit retry with idempotent action IDs). False positive confirmations (Critical/Prevent by forbidding optimistic success and no terminal labels without server ack). Trust boundary abuse via open pod membership links (Medium/Mitigate by invite-only join, creator-issued codes, and membership checks on every write). Growth failure due to first-incident fragility (High/Mitigate by two-device incident acceptance as primary release gate). **Claude (QA & Risk · Skeptic) — Round 1**

Let me stress-test this before it goes into architecture, because several of the "trust graph" and "server-arbitrated" guarantees we've locked have real edge cases that could quietly break them in practice.

The one I'd put first: what happens when a pod member has denied notification permission, or has Focus/DND on and hasn't paid for the critical-alert tier we locked as a paid unlock? We've built the entire growth thesis around "the core loop works flawlessly on every pod's first real incident," but the free tier's core mechanism for pod members finding out about a request *is* the push notification — and we've explicitly reserved DND-bypass for paying users. That means the single most likely failure mode for a brand-new pod's first incident is: parent posts request, three pod members have their phones in a drawer or in Focus mode, nobody sees it in time, the parent gives up and goes back to the group chat, and that pod's word-of-mouth growth is dead before it started. I don't think this is solvable in v1, but it needs to be named as a real limitation, not quietly assumed away — the client should show the poster something honest like "delivered to N pod members" rather than implying "everyone was notified," because we don't actually know they saw it.

Second: what does "same-day" mean when it's checked, and whose clock decides it? If a request is posted at 11:58pm, or a co-parenting pod has members in different time zones (which is a realistic edge case for exactly the custody-documentation use case we built the receipt export for), device-local midnight is the wrong boundary. I'd resolve this by having the server stamp everything in UTC and defining "same-day" as relative to the pod's home time zone (set once at pod creation), never per-device — otherwise elapsed-time and still-open aging becomes ambiguous exactly when it matters most.

Third, and this feels underspecified given how much weight we've put on "no ambiguity, ever": what happens to an open request if the requester force-quits the app, loses network, or the app crashes right after posting, before the client gets a "delivered" ack? Does the request exist on the server already, in a queued local draft, or both? We need an explicit idempotency guarantee here — a retry of the same post action must not create two live requests for the same incident, and a client relaunch must reconcile against server truth rather than assume its last local state. Same problem on the accept side: if a device force-quits between tapping accept and receiving the server's CAS result, on relaunch it must re-fetch and show the real outcome, not whatever the UI was mid-transition when it died. This needs to be a named test case alongside the two-phone race demo, not something we discover during QA.

Fourth: the join-code/invite-link mechanism is the entire enforcement of "trust graph, not strangers," and it's also the weakest link in that promise. A join code is just a string — it can be screenshotted and forwarded outside the pod, posted somewhere, or reused indefinitely if we don't expire or single-use it. If a code leaks, the trust-graph safety property we spent a whole phase locking becomes decorative. I think we need an explicit decision here, not left implicit: are codes single-use, time-limited, or revocable, and does the pod creator (who otherwise has zero admin capability in v1) have any way to invalidate a compromised code? If the answer is "no, codes are permanent and un-revocable," that's a real, nameable risk we should write down as an accepted limitation rather than something that quietly wasn't thought about.

Fifth: a pod of size one. The creator creates a pod and, before anyone else joins, posts a request (or just explores the app). There's no one to notify. This isn't a hypothetical — it's the default state of every brand-new pod for however long it takes the second family to accept an invite. The empty/loading states we're required to build for every screen need to explicitly distinguish "your request is live but nobody's in your pod yet to see it" from "your request is live and pending pod response" — those are very different situations and collapsing them into one generic "waiting" state recreates exactly the false-confidence problem this whole app exists to prevent.

Sixth: the shared audit/receipt object raises a data-ownership question we haven't touched. If it's evidence two parties may rely on (including for custody documentation, which we explicitly designed the export feature for), can either party unilaterally delete their account and take that record down, or does it need to survive independently of either individual account since it documents something that happened between two people? I'd propose the audit record is retained and viewable by both original parties even if one deletes their account, with only PII-adjacent profile data (name shown on it) handled via a "deleted user" placeholder rather than cascading deletion of the whole record — otherwise a parent could unilaterally erase evidence the other parent is relying on.

Last one, more of a product-honesty risk than a technical one: nothing in the architecture verifies that an accepter is actually capable of making the pickup in time — no location, which was correctly rejected for privacy/scope reasons, but it means "accepted" only ever means "a trusted person has claimed responsibility," not "help is confirmed to arrive in time." If an accepter claims it, then can't make it and has to release with only a few minutes left, the app did exactly what it promised (explicit reversible state, re-notify) but the outcome can still be bad. That's an acceptable and correctly-scoped limitation given everything already decided, but I want it written down as an explicit assumption in this phase's output so nobody downstream mistakes "accepted" for "arrival guaranteed."
